Assistance to fiscal deficit States 
*222. SHRI SURENDRA LATH: Will the Minist er of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have a proposal to rescue the revenue deficit States 
from financial crisis; 
(b) the State-wise financial condition at the moment; and 
(c) the steps taken to assist the revenue  deficit States for improving their 
financial condition? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI JASWANT SINGH): (a) to (c) A 
Statement is placed on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (c) Yes, Sir. The Government has initiated several measures in this 
regard. Apart from the release of non-plan revenue deficit grant as 
recommended by the Eleventh Finance Commision, Government of India also 
extends need-based assistance to States , so as to take care of temporary 
mismatch in their receipt and expenditures. 
3 

RAJYA  SABHA [5 August, 2003] 
Further, in order to supplement the efforts of the State Governments towards 
fiscal consolidation, Government of Indi a, has also created a "States' Fiscal 
Reforms Facility (2000-01 to 2004-05)". This facility provides incentives to 
States to undertake Medium-Term Fiscal Reforms Programme (MTFRP), 
which aims at reducing their revenue and gross fiscal deficits, over the reform 
period. 
In addition, Government of India, has also introduced a debt-swap 
scheme to enable States to retire th eir high cost borrowings by taking 
advantage of the current low-interest regime. 
Government of India has also assisted some State Governments to avail 
multilateral institutional funding for undertaking fiscal and structural reforms.

*224. SHRIMATI BIMBA RAIKAR: Will the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Indian companies listed on the US bourses are likely to be 
adversely impacted under the Genera lly Accepted Accounting Principles

corporate accounting norms in te rms of recording Employee Stock 
Ownership Plans transactions;

found to be adversely affected by the GAAP system, although it recorded profits 
in Indian operations; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI JASWANT SINGH): (a) to (d) A 
Statement is placed on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) Companies listed in the US can follow one of the two 
pronouncements prescribed under the US GAAP Accounting for ESOPs., viz 
Intrinsic Value method or Fair Value method. Indian companies, presently 
following the Intrinsic Value method of Accounting for ESOPs, if required to 
follow the Fair Value method in the US may be adversely affected. As per the 
SEBI, ESOP guidelines 1999, an option to follow either the Intrinsic Value 
method or the Fair Value method is open to Indian Companies.

Water storage capacity 
*230.SHRI R.K.ANAND: Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be 
pleased to state; 
(a) whether it is a fact that Indi a receives a surface water flow of 
1869 billion cubic metre and the capacity to store water including the 
ongoing project is only 420 billion cubic metre; 
(b) whether Government have formulated any plan to make 
arrangements to store water and to prevent the water flowing back into 
the sea; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI ARJUN CHARAN 
SETHI): (a) The annual average flow in the river systems of the country is 
1869 Billion Cubic Metre (BCM). Owing to the topographic, hydrological and 
other constraints, the utilizable water is 1122 BCM of which, surface water is 
690 BCM and annual replenishable ground water resource is 432 BCM. Till 
now, total live storage capacity of 177  BCM has been created. An additional 
live storage capacity of 75 BCM will be created on completion of the 
ongoing projects. Another live storage capacity of 132 BCM is to be created 
through the projects under consideration. 
(b) and (c) In order to store the water, schemes are planned, investigated, 
formulated, implemented and funded by  the respective State Governments 
out of their own resources and as per their own priorities. An additional live 
storage capacity of 75 BCM will be created on completion of the ongoing 
projects. For speedy completion of ongoing water resources projects, the 
Central Government has launched th e Accelerated Irrigation Benefits 
Programme (AIBP). Under the programme, financial assistance in form of 
central loan is being extended to State Governments to help thorn complete the 
ongoing irrigation projects in a time bound manner so that the benefits could 
accrue at the earliest. Besides, live storage capacity of 132 BCM is to be 
created through the projects under consideration. Government of India is also 
promoting rain water harvesting through Watershed Management 
Programme, artificial recharge of ground water and roof -top rain water 
harvesting under the sector reform project of Accelerated Rural Water Supply 
Programme under the Ministry of Rural Development, for which 
35 

RAJYA SABHA [5 August, 2003] 
technical and financial assistance is provided to the State Governments and 
other implementing agencies. Central Ground Water Board has also taken up 
a Central Sector Scheme on "Studies of Recharge to Ground Water" on pilot 
basis. Central Ground Water Board has prepared a "Master Plan for Artificial 
Recharge to Ground Water" which envisages to recharge 36453 Million Cubic 
Metre volume of water through 2.25 lakhs artificial recharge structures in 
rural areas like percolation tanks, check dams, sub-surface dykes, gully plugs, 
gabion structures, nala bunds, contour bunds, recharge shafts etc. As a long 
term measure, National Water Development Agency have formulated 
National Perspective Plan for water re sources development which envisages 
interlinking various Peninsular rivers and Himalayan rivers.

1688. SHRI S. P. M. SYED KHAN: Will the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether the appreciation in value of rupee against US Dollar is 
market driven or RBI influenced one; 
(b) whether the appreciation in rupee is beneficial to the economy; 
(c) what steps are being taken to consolidate the gains made by rupee in 
the recent past; and 
(d) what is it's effect on Indian software industry and manufacturing 
industry? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE 
(SHRI ANANDRAO VITHOBA ADSUL): (a) The exchange rate of the 
Rupee is determined by market fo rces since March 1993. The primary 
objective of the Reserve Bank of India with regard to the management of the 
exchange rate is maintenance of orderly conditions in the forex market, and 
meeting temporary demand supply gaps, which may arise due to uncertainty or 
other reasons, without focusing on any target rate. 
(b) The appreciation/depreciation of the Rupee has its own 
advantages/disadvantages for different sectors of the economy. The 
main objective of the Reserve Bank of India in managing the exchange 
rate is to ensure that the economic fundamentals are reflected in the 
exchange rate of the Rupee and undue volatility in the forex market is 
contained in the interest of real-sector stability. 
(c) The exchange rate of the Rupee depends on a variety of factors, 
including demand and supply conditions in the forex market, 
developments at home and abroad etc. In recent times, Rupee has 
been appreciating against the US Dollar, which has more to do with the 
weakness of the US economy. The Reserve Bank of India has been 
adopting an attitude of watchfulness, caution and flexibility by closely 
monitoring the developments in the financial markets at home and abroad 
and co-ordinate its market operations carefully in the area of exchange 
rate management.

other than the promoters' contribution, could be raised through public 
issue or private placement. In case the promoters' contribution to the 
initial capital is in excess of the minimum proportion of 40 per cent, 
they shall dilute their excess stake after one year of the bank's 
operations. (In case divestment after one year is proposed to be spread 
over a period of time, this would require specific approval of the 
RBI). Promoters' contribution of 40% of the initial capital shall be 
locked in for a period of five years from the date of licensing of the 
bank. 
(iii) While augmenting capital to Rs . 300 crore within three years of 
commencement of business, the promoters will have to bring in 
additional capital, which would be at least 40 per cent of the fresh 
capital raised. The remaining portion could be raised through public 
issue or private placement. The promoters' contribution of a minimum 
of 40% of additional capital will also be locked in for a . minimum 
period of 5 years from the date of receipt of capital by the bank. 
(iv) NRI participation in the primary equity of a new bank shall be to the 
maximum extent of 40 per cent. In the case of a foreign banking 
company or finance company (including multilateral institutions) as a 
technical collaborator or a co-promoter, equity participation shall be 
restricted to 20 per cent within the above ceiling of 40 per cent. In 
cases of shortfall in foreign equity contributions by NRIs, designated 
multilateral institutions would be allowed to contribute foreign equity 
to the extent of the shortfall in NRI contribution to the equity. The 
proposed bank shall obtain 
96 

[5 August, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
necessary approval of Foreign Investment Promotion Board of the 
Government of India and Exchange Control Department of RBI. 
(v) The new bank should not be promoted by a large industrial house. 
However, individual companies, dir ectly or indirectly connected with 
large industrial houses may be permitted to participate in the equity of 
a new private sector bank up to a maximum of 10 per cent but will not 
have controlling interest in the bank. The 10 per cent limit would 
apply to all inter-connected companies belonging to the concerned 
large industrial houses. In taking a view on whether the companies, 
either as promoters or investors, belong to a large industrial house or to 
a company connected to a large industrial house, the decision of the 
RBI will be final. 
(vi) The proposed bank shall maintain an arms length relationship with 
business entities in the promoter group and the individual 
company/ies investing upto 10% promoters and company/ies investing 
up to 10 per cent of the equity. The relationship between business 
entities in the promoter group and the proposed bank shall be of a 
similar nature as between two independent and unconnected entities. 
In taking view on whether a company belongs to a particular 
Promoter Group or not, the decision of RBI shall be final. 
(vii)  Conversion of NBFCs into private sector banks 
An NBFC with a good track record desiring conversion into a bank 
should satisfy the following criteria: 
• The NBFC should have a minimum net worth of Rs. 200 crore in its 
latest balance sheet which will stand increased to Rs. 300 crore within 
three years from the date of conversion. 
• The NBFC should not have been promoted by a large Industrial House 
or owned/controlled by public authorities, including Local, State or 
Central Governments. 
• The NBFC should have acquired a credit rating of not less than AAA 
rating (or its equivalent) in the previous year. 
• The NBFC should have an impeccable track record in compliance 
97 

RAJYA SABHA [5 August, 2003] 
with RBI regulations/directions and in repayment of public deposits and 
no default should have been reported. 
• The NBFC desiring conversion into bank should have capital 
adequacy of not less than 12 per cent and net NPAs of not more than 5 
per cent. 
• The NBFC on conversion to a bank will have to comply with Capital 
Adequacy Ratio and all other requirements such as lending to priority 
sector, promoters' contribution, lock-in period for promoters' stake, 
dilution of promoters' stake beyond the minimum, NRI and foreign 
equity participation, arms length relationship, etc. as applicable to 
banks. 
3. Other Requirements 
(i) The bank shall be required to maintain a minimum capital adequacy 
ratio of 10 per cent on a continuous basis from the commencement of 
its operations. 
(ii)   In order to ensure level playing field, 
(a) the new bank will have to observe priority sector lending target of 40 
per cent of net bank credit as applicable to other domestic banks, and 
(b) the new bank will be required to op en 25 per cent of its branches in 
rural and semi-urban areas to avoid over concentration of their 
branches in metropolitan areas and cities on the same lines as new 
private sector banks established under guidelines laid down by RBI in 
January 1993, 
(iii) the promoters, their group companies and the proposed bank shall 
accept the system of consolidated supervision by the Reserve Bank of 
India. 
(iv) The new bank shall not be allowed to set up a subsidiary or mutual 
fund for at least three years from  the date of commencement of 
business. 
(v) The headquarters of the proposed new bank could be in any location in 
India as decided by the promoters. 
(vi) The new bank shall make full use of modern infrastructural facilities in 
office equipments, computer, telecommunications etc. in order to 
provide cost-effective customer service. It should have 
98 

[5 August, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
a high powered Customer Grievances Cell to handle customer 
complaints. 
(vii) The new bank will be governed by the provisions of the Banking 
Regulation Act, 1949, Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, other 
relevant Statutes and the Directives, Prudential regulations and other 
Guidelines/Instructions issued by RBI and the regulations of SEBI 
regarding public issues and other guidelines applicable to listed 
banking companies. 
4. Procedure for Applications 
(i) In terms of Rule 11 of the Banking Regulation (Companies) Rules, 1949 
applications shall be submitted in the prescribed form (Form III). In 
addition, the applications should furnish a project report covering 
business potential and viability of the proposed bank, the business 
focus, the product lines, proposed regional or locational spread, level 
of information technol ogy capability and any other information that 
they consider relevant. The project  r e p o r t  s h o u l d  g i v e  a s  m u c h  
concrete details as feasible, based on adequate ground level 
information and avoid unrealistic or unduly ambitious projections. 
Applications should also be supported by detailed information on the 
background of promoters, their expertise, track record of business and 
financial worth, details of promoters'  direct and indirect interests in 
various companies/industries, details of credit/other facilities availed 
by the promoters/promoter company(ies)/other Group company (ies) 
with banks/financial institutions, and details of proposed participation 
by foreign banks/NRI/OCBs. 
(ii) Applications for setting up new banks in the private sector, along with 
other details as mentioned above, should reach the following address 
before March 31. 2001. 
The Chief General Manager-in-Charge, 
Department of Banking Operations and Development, 
Reserve Bank of India, 
World Trade Centre, Centre I, 
Cuffe Parade, Colaba,

5. Procedure for RBI decisions 
(i) In view of the increasing emphasis on stringent prudential norms, 
transparency, disclosure requirements and modern technology, the new 
banks need to have strength and efficiency to work profitably in a 
highly competitive environment. As a number of banks are already 
functioning, licences will be issued on a very selective basis to those 
who conform to the above requirements and who are likely to conform 
to the best international and domestic standards of customer service 
and efficiency. Preference will howev er be given to promoters with 
expertise of financing priority areas and in setting up banks 
specialising in the financing of rural and agro based industries. The 
number of licences to be issued in the next three years may be restricted 
to two or three of the best acceptable proposals. This number would also 
include permission granted to any NBFC for conversion into bank. (If 
the number of acceptable proposals of  the highest standards are more 
than three, this limit may be relaxed on recommendation of the 
Advisory Committee (see below). In that case the period for issuing 
new licences may be stretched to four or five years). 
(ii) At the first stage, the applicati ons will be screened by RBI to ensure 
prima facie eligibility of the applicants. Thereafter, the applications 
will be referred to a high-level Advisory Committee to be set up the 
RBI comprising. 
Dr. I.G. Patel, former Governor of

Shri C.G. Somiah, former Comptroller and 
Auditor General of India —    Member 
Shri Dipankar Basu, former Chairman of 
State Bank of India —    Member 
Chief General Manager of the Department of Banking Operations and 
Development of RBI will be the Secretary of the Advisory Committee. 
(iii)  The Committee will set up its own procedures for screening the 
applications. The Committee will reserve the right to call for more 
information as well as have discussions with any applicant/s and 
   seek clarification on any issue as required by it. The Committee

months after the last date of receipt of applications by RBI (i.e. 30

of a bank will be taken by RBI. RBI's decision will be final. 
(iv) The validity of the in-principle approval issued by RBI will be one year 
from the date of granting in-principle approval and would thereafter

(v) After issue of the in-principle approval for setting up of a bank in the

Study on Seismic Survey 
1749. SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT: Will the Minister of PETROLEUM 
AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that in certai n areas where earlier seismic surveys 
conducted by ONGC, OIL, and others failed to locate presence of 
hydrocarbons have shown positive results  by subsequent surveys conducted 
by private sector enterprises; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether any study has been conducted to go into the causes for the 
failure of earlier surveys; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PETROLEUM 
AND NATURAL GAS (SHRIMATI SUMITRA MAHAJAN): (a) to (e) At 
present, it is only after drilling of a well and production testing that the 
presence of hydrocarbons, crude oil and/or natural gas, is established. Various 
kinds of surveys, such as Gravity Magnetic and Seismic, only serve to 
indicate some probability of occurence of hydrocarbons. The success in 
discovery of hydrocarbons depends inter alia on the geological model of the area, 
which in turn keeps on getting refine d with technological advancement and 
fresh data input. As such, revisiting exploratory acreages with refined models 
is an Upstream practice all over the world. Oil and natural gas discoveries 
have been made with improvement in technology, changes in geological 
insights after initial failures. As such, no adverse inference may be drawn about 
these failures nor is any study requisite.

Demand and supply of water 
1781. SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that during the last 50 years India has been 
reduced from a water-rich country to a water scarce country; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(c) the steps proposed to be taken to reverse the trend and take back the 
country to its original position and reduce the mismatch between the demand and 
supply of water? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) The annual 
average flow in the river systems of the country is 1869 Billion Cubic Metre 
(BCM). The per capita water availability in 1951 was 5177 cubic metre per 
year. With growth of population from 361 million in 1951 to 1027 million in 
2001, the per capita water availability reduced to 1820 cubic metre per year. 
Due to variation in rainfall in space and time, the availability of water also 
varies from basin to basin in the country and in some of the basins, the per 
capita water availability is less than 1000 cubic metre per year. As per 
international criteria, a situation of annual per capita availability of water of less 
than 1000 cubic metre is considered as scarcity condition. 
(b) The rapid growth of population has led to lesser per capita 
availability of water. 
158 

[5 August, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) Due to rapid growth of population, urbanisation and improved 
standards of living, the demand of water has considerably increased. Various 
schemes, particularly storage schemes have already been completed with a 
view to reduce the gap between demand and availability. The live storage 
capacity created so far is about 177 BCM. Additional storage capacity of 75 
BCM will be created on completion of projects which are under various stages 
of construction. Proposals for a dditional projects are also under 
formulation/consideration for creation of storage capacity of 132 BCM. To 
accelerate creation of irrigation potential by early completion of ongoing 
schemes, Government of India has launched Accelerated Irrigation benefits 
Programme (AIBP).Government of India is also promoting rainwater 
harvesting through Watershed Management Programme, artificial recharge of 
ground water and roof-top rainwater harvesting under the sector reform 
project of Accelerated Rural Water Supply Programme of the Ministry of 
Rural Development, for which technical and financial assistance is provided to 
the State Govaanments and other implementing agencies. Central Ground 
Water Board has also taken up a Central Sector Scheme on "Studies of 
Recharge to Ground Water" on pilot basis. For meeting future requirements of 
water, as a long term measure, National Water Development Agency have 
formulated National Perspective Plan for water resources development which 
envisages interlinking various Peninsular rivers and Himalayan rivers.

envisages that exploitation of ground water resources should be so

regulated as not to exceed the recharging possibilities. It further envisages 
that the detrimental environmental consequences of over-exploitation of

Failure of civic agencies to use water 
1788. SHRI RAJU PARMAR: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether about 80 per cent of the 380 million gallons of water treated 
every day is released into the river as none of the civic agencies has the 
infrastructure to utilize it; 
(b) if so, what are the details thereof; and 
(c) the action Government propose to take to recycle this water for use by 
various civic agencies? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) to (b) A study by 
the Central Pollution Control Board in 1994-95 shows that the total waste-
water generated in 300 Class-I cities is about 15,800 million litres a day (mid), 
while the treatment capacity is hardly 3,750 mld. In the 23 metro cities, over 
9000 million litres of sewage is generated daily, of which a bout 60 per cent is 
generated in the four mega cities of Mumbai, Kolkata, Delhi and Chennai. Of 
the total waste water generated in the metro cities, hardly 30 per cent is 
treated before disposal. Most of the cities have only primary treatment 
facilities. Thus, the untreated and 
167 

RAJYA SABHA [5 August, 2003] 
partially treated municipal waste water finds its way into water sources such 
as rivers, lakes and ground water. 
(c) Urban Water Supply and Sanitation being a State subject, it is the 
responsibility of the State Government and Urban Local Bodies to plan, 
implement, execute, operate, monitor schemes and make adequate "provision in 
their annual budgets. 
The 10th Plan Document inter-alia suggests the measures of recycling of 
treated waste water as part of conservation measures and the suggested action 
points are as under: 
"Reuse of treated sewage must be given priority in view of the fact that 
water is going to become more scarce in the near future. With tertiary treatment, 
water from treated sewage can be used even for air-conditioning, industrial 
and non-potable uses. This must be made thrust area". 
• The treated waste water may be used  extensively in agriculture and 
horticulture. 
• Depending upon the local conditions , appropriate systems must be 
selected to treat the municipal waste water in urban areas; 
• Wherever sufficient land is available, simple treatment systems such 
as stabilization pond, duckweed pond, artificial wet lands etc. may be 
adopted to treat and dispose the municipal waste water; 
• In large housing complexes, and townships, on-site waste water 
treatment such as septic tank, soak pits etc. may be adopted. 
Schemes for flood control 
†1789. SHRI ABHAY KANT PRASAD: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether devastating floods occur due to the several rivers originating 
from the Himalaya and flowing through various parts of the country 
particularly Bihar, Jharkhand, Assam and North-Eastern region; 
(b) whether Government have any proposal/scheme to control such type of 
flood; and 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
168 

[5 August, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) if so, the details thereof including the details of the scheme 
formulated with the help of World Bank and other agencies for this purpose, 
State-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) Yes, Sir. Several 
rivers including Ganga, Brahmaputra and their tributaries orginating from 
Himalaya cause floods in the State of Bihar, Assam and other North-Eastern 
States of the country. As regards the State of Jharkhand, flood problem is not 
reported to be acute although some erosion problems are reported in the main 
Ganga river down stream of Sahebganj area. 
(b) to (c) Flood Management being a State subject, the flood control 
schemes are planned, funded and executed by the State Government 
themselves as per their priorities and availability of funds for the purpose. 
However, the Central Government has also been taking various 
measures for assisting the States in the management of flood, some of which 
are briefly discussed here under: 
Ganga and Brahmaputra basins are the severely flood affected regions in 
the country. The Ganga Flood Control Commission constituted by the Central 
Government in 1972 had prepared comprehensive plans for flood management 
for all the 23 river systems of Gang a Basin. Similarly, the Brahmaputra 
Board constituted in 1982 under an act of Parliament has also prepared 
Master Plans for the Brahmaputra and Barak Basins. These reports/Master 
Plans were forwarded to the concerned States for formulating schemes for 
implementation after detailed investigations. 
In addition, the Government of India also constituted a number of 
Committees/Task Force/Expert Groups including setting up of Rashtriya Barh 
Ayog in 1976 to study the various issues relating to Flood Management, the 
recommendations of which have been sent to the State Governments for 
taking follow up action. 
As a non-structural measure, a nationwide flood forecasting and warning 
system has been established by the Central Water Commission which issues 
flood forecasts at 161 statio ns in the country of which 134 stations are for 
river stage forecast and 27 of inflow forecast. 
An agreement has also been reached with Nepal and the Government of 
India has approved a scheme for setting up of Joint Project 
169 

RAJYA SABHA [5 August, 2003] 
Office to take up field investigations, studies and preparation of Detailed Project 
Report of Sapata Kosi High Dam Multipurpose Project and Sun Kosi Storage 
cum Diversion Scheme. The project inter alia will have flood control 
benefits for the State of Bihar. 
In furtherance to the Master Plan prepared by the Brahmaputra Board for 
effective flood control in North East on a long term basis and to exploit the large 
hydro-electric potential available in Brahmaputra Valley, investigations of 
two projects namely the Siang (Dihang) Dam Project and the Subansiri Dam 
Project were pursued and project reports were prepared by the Brahmaputra 
Board. These projects, which are now to be taken up in three stages each, have 
since been transferred to National Hydro-electric Power Corporation (NHPC). 
NHPC has already initiated action for execution of Lower Subansiri Dam 
Project, while other projects are under various stages of 
investigations/implementation by NHPC. 
For flood control benefits in Assam the Government of India have 
approved the following schemes, which have been taken up for 
implementation by the Brahmaputra Board: 
(i)   Pagladiya Dam Project with an estimated cost of Rs. 542.90 crore. 
(ii)   Harrang Drainage Development Scheme at an estimated cost of Rs. 
30.49 crore. 
(iii)  Avulsion of Brahmaputra river at Dholla Hathighulli at an estimated cost 
of Rs. 10.47 crore. 
In addition the Government of India has also been providing financial 
assistance under the Central Sector/Centrally Sponsored Schemes to the 
various State Governments to take up critical anti-erosion and other flood 
management works. 
However, at present there is no Central scheme for flood control 
formulated with the help of World Bank.

SPECIAL MENTIONS 
Need to provide special package for development of NH-6 between 
Sambalpur and Bargarh in Orissa 
MS. PRAMILA BOHIDAR (Orissa): Mr. Chairman, Sir, all the 
National Highways are lifeline of the nation. They are like veins and arteries. It 
should be so in the case of NH-6 which passes through Sambalpur 
connecting Mumbai and Kolkata. 
NH-6, as on today, remains a two- lane way, even though it goes 
through the densest industrial and agricultural belt in Orissa. 
Between Bargarh and Sambalpur, it serves the industrial towns of 
Bargarh, Burla, Hirakud, Sambalpur and even the peripheral Jharsuguda-
Belpahar zone of the Mahanadi Coalfiel ds Ltd. (MCL). Needless to say, the 
mines and minerals, finished products like iron, aluminium, coal, etc. are 
carried through this National Highway. The Bargarh-Atabira belt is considered 
the rice bowl of Orissa and the FCI procures and stores paddy by hauling 
them through NH-6. 
Sambalpur-Hirakud-Burla areas house one university, one 
engineering and medical college each, apart from the Hirakud Irrigation Canal 
Systern, No wonder, the traffic on NH-6 is swelling and density of vehicles and 
road users is increasing day by day. Congestion on roads and causalities due 
to accidents are increasing. Most of the road accident victims on NH-6 
between Bargarh and Ainthapali Junction near Sambalpur are in the age 
group of 18-40, which is the most productive span in a man's lifetime. 
196 

[5 August, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
The Minister for Road Transport and Highways had announced that 
Rs. 7.57 crores would be spent on improving the riding quality of roads in 
three phases between September 2002 and June 2003. I urge upon the hon. 
Minister to urgently take up four-laning of NH-6 between Sambalpur and 
Bargarh as a special package on priority basis during the current financial 
year so that trade and commerce can gr ow and precious lives are not lost 
further in gruesome road accidents. 
Need to ban wax coating on Fruits and Vegetables 
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA (Rajasthan): Sir, as Shri Suresh 
Pachouri has just now talked about milk, I want to talk about fruits and 
vegetables. 
Whether the Government is willing to take the responsibility of health 
of crores of citizens is a big questi on. The use of wax by traders and vendors 
to polish fruits and vegetables to make them shining and attractive and 
preserving the moisture inside to minimize wastage and increase the profit 
are old practices and the Government has been aware of it for a long time. 
Edible wax is imported from U SA and other European countries and 
most of the vendors in Indi a are not in a position to import wax from these 
countries. Naturally, they would use the alternative wax which is commonly 
available in Indian markets. 
As stated by Shri S. R. Gupta, Director-General, PFA, there are two 
types of waxes, edible and non-edible. But in India, there is no guarantee that 
the correct one will be used and many people do not even wash or peel the 
fruits before eating. Even the Health Mi nistry believes that wax coating could 
be adulterated with chemicals harmful to health. However, the concept of 
fresh fruits and vegetables is liquidated by  the use of wax. Naturally, it is the 
health of crores of people that the Government should worry about rather than 
the handful who use it and make profit out of it. 
Therefore, I urge upon the Governm ent to immediately ban the use 
of wax on fruits and vegetables till some kind of a guarantee is given that only 
safe and edible wax would be used in future.

SHRI EDUARDO FALEIRO (Goa): Mr. Chairman, Sir, a uniform civil 
code is not feasible in India, unless and until an atmosphere of communal 
harmony prevails, and every community is confident that its religious and 
cultural identity is not threatened. We have the Special Marriage Act, 1954. It 
is a 'uniform civil code of marriage'. But very few opt for marriage under this 
Act. All Indian communities are tradition-bound, and marriages are 
solemnized under different personal laws. It is sometimes said that the 
Uniform Civil Code, existing in Goa should be a model for the rest of the 
country. This is a gross misconcepti on. The legalisation in Goa is the 
Portuguese Civil Code, which was extended to Goa in 1870 during the 
colonial rule. It is entirely based on the Western Christian jurisprudence. In

expenditure. This is a luxury which the country can't afford at this juncture. We 
have to come out of this situation. If the same trend continues, many social 
problems are sure to come. I don't want to be a Prophet of

DR. V. MAITREYAN (Tamil Nadu): Madam Deputy Chairperson, 
representing a regional party, especially the ruling party, I shall focus on the 
problems faced by us, what we have done in the last two years or so and what 
we expect from the Union Finance Minister. 
Since the mid 1990s, the public finances of Tamil Nadu have shown 
extremely disturbing trends. On the one hand, the revenue expenditure, 
comprising commitments on salaries, pensions, interest payments, subsidies 
and grants has shown a phenomenal increase. And, on the other, the revenue 
receipts did not keep pace with the unprecedented increase in the revenue 
expenditure, resulting in worsening the revenue deficit. Added to this, a higher 
level of borrowings, primarily intended to meet the revenue deficit, has added 
to the problem and has also led to a worsening of the fiscal deficit. 
242 

[5 August, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
Following the recommendations of the Eleventh Finance 
Commission, Tamil Nadu's share in the divisible pool of Central Taxes is 
reduced by an estimated amount of Rs . 2,946 crores for the period 2000-
2005. Further, the Government of Indi a reduced its promised devolution of 
Central taxes by a further amount of Rs. 540 crores in 2001-2002, and Rs. 
274.50 crores in 2002-2003, due to poor collection of the Central taxes. This 
has further exacerbated the already worse financial situation. 
After the AIADMK Government, led by hon. Chief Mi nister, Dr. J. 
Jayalalithaaji, assumed office in May, 2001, we had undertaken a series of 
major fiscal reforms, covering the revenue expenditure as well as the revenue 
receipts of the State. Madam, under th e Chairmanship of Dr. Raja J. Chelliah, 
Tax Reforms and Revenue Augmentation Commission was constituted to 
increase the tax and non-tax revenues, and to streamline the tax 
administration system in the Stat e, and its interim report has been 
incorporated in the Budget for this y ear. The last year's Budget indicated an 
additional resource mobilization, throug h changes in taxation, of nearly Rs. 
690 crores and this has yielded very good results for us. 
The Samadhan Scheme, for settling th e stamp duty dues in disputed 
cases, has yielded additional revenue of Rs. 100 crores last year. Due to an 
intensive checking, enforcement and bette r collection, the Sales Tax, last 
year, has increased 15 per cent over t he previous year. This year's Budget 
provides for an additional resource mobilization of nearly Rs. 480 crores. Also, 
on non-tax side, such as forests, i rrigation, mines and minerals have all 
improved. With reference to revenue expenditure, as an economy measure, 
certain benefits to the Government Employees, such as encashment of leave, 
payment of bonus, etc., have been curtailed. The burden imposed by new 
instalments of Dearness Allowance has been handled by making the payment 
with a lag. The Government has constituted a Staff and Expenditure Reforms 
Commission, headed by Dr A.M. Swaminathan, a retired I.A.S. officer. Based 
on the identified surplus posts, abolit ion of equivalent posts is being 
undertaken. And, the Government has taken a committed decision that new 
recruitment in Government is totally banned with effect from November 2001, 
except a few essential categories such  as police, doctors and teachers. The 
Government has already announced a new Contributory Pension Scheme 
which will be applicable to selected categories of new employees who are 
employed w.e.f. 1st April, 2003. Also, other pension entitlements have been 
introduced

SHRI SURENDRA LATH (Orissa): Madam, thank you very much for 
giving me the opportunity to participate in this important debate on the 
financial health of the States. This is  a very important matter. The rapid 
deterioration in the condition of the State finances is an issue of serious 
concern. The devastating financial cond ition has been an important constraint 
in creating quality infrastructure and development and reduces the investment 
in social sectors. 
Madam, the gross fiscal deficit of t he States is increasing every year. 
The total gross fiscal deficit of the States in 2001-02 rose to Rs. 1,06,595 
crores, which is 4.3 per cent of the GD P. This is because of a decrease in 
revenue receipts and an increase in reve nue expenditure. The States have to 
resort to a high level of borrowings to meet the increased revenue 
expenditure. This causes increase in large scale fiscal revenue deficit. The 
high magnitude of interest payment pr e-empts revenue receipts, thereby put 
constraints on developmental activities of the States. 
Madam, there are various reasons for this state of affairs. A very 
significant reason is the enormous increase in the wage bills and pension 
liabilities. After the implementation of  the recommendations of the Fifth Pay 
Commission, the wage bills of the Stat es increased to a great extent. The 
share of revenue deficit increased from 38 per cent in 1997-98, to 60 per cent, 
in 1998-99 due to the pay revision. T he pension liabilities of the States have 
also shown a sharp rise, and it also enhanced the revenue expenditure to a 
large extent. The fiscal deficit which was 3 per cent of the GDP, in 1997-
98,.increased sharply to 4.2 per cent, in 1998-99 and 4.6 per cent in 
1999-2000. 
288 

[5 August, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
Secondly, Madam, the State Gove rnments have also invested large 
sums in public sector undertakings, but t he receipts from these public sector 
undertakings in the form of dividend and pr ofit is negligible. Most of the State 
public sector undertakings are making huge losses and need budgetary 
support, which causes an additional burden on the State finances. Most of the 
State Electricity Boards were making huge losses due to a large amount of 
subsidy given by some States. 
Madam, the other reason for financial indiscipline is that the 
outstanding guarantees issued by the State Governments have risen in the 
recent years. There is an additional burden on the State finances due to a 
default by the entities for whom t he guarantees have been issued. The non-
adherence to the payment obligation committed by the States in respect of the 
guarantee already provided by them has adverse implications on the 
sovereign credibility, and, thus, may create problems in future, in raising 
resources from the market. Because of these reasons, many States have put 
a ceiling on issuing guarantees in order to restrict the increase in the debt 
burden of the States. 
Madam, because of the financial constraints and the increase in 
revenue expenditure and spending on unproductive expenditure, there is little 
left for making a provision for expenditure for development and other social 
services. There is a decline in the Pl an expenditure on health, education, 
agriculture and industry, infrastructure development and other social sectors. 
In the above sectors, the total disburseme nt in the Sixth Plan was 5.1% of the 
GDP; in the Seventh Plan, it was 5.1%, in the Eighth Plan, it was 4.2%. and it 
was reduced to 3.7% in the Ninth Plan period. The whole situation is very 
alarming and needs an improvement in the financial condition of the States. 
Madam, the Government has set a target of 8% growth rate in the 
Tenth Plan period. In order to achieve th e target, it is urgently required to 
strengthen the economy of the States. To achieve this, there is an urgent need 
to implement the physical reforms pr ogram. There is a need for reducing the 
revenue expenditure, and. thereby, also reducing the revenue deficit. It is also 
required to reduce the debt burden of the States by reducing the interest 
component. 
Madam, there is a need for making a readjustment across several 
areas of Government finances. Improvement in the management of public 
expenditure and comprehensive civil service reforms for improving public 
289 

RAJYA SABHA [5 August, 2003] 
service delivery through increased accountability, integrity and productivity of 
the civil services is also required. 
There is a need for reducing the bu rden of revenue deficit and fiscal 
deficit through reducing the wasteful expenditure, cutting the low priority 
expenditure and raising the efficiency of the tax administration and the tax 
regime is the basic objective of the readjustment programme. 
As we know, the State Electricity Boards are making huge losses. 
There is a need for introducing power sector reforms which can reduce the 
negative contribution to the State's revenue. Many States have already 
introduced the power sector reforms. 
Madam, the public sector restructur ing is an essential part of the 
physical reforms. The loss-making public sector undertakings should be either 
disinvested or privatised.  The State Governments should restrict giving a 
budgetary support to the loss-making companies. 
Madam, the Eleventh Finance Commission has set the physical 
objectives. Chapter 30 of the main Repo rt lays down the broad parameters of 
the physical correction in the State se ctor starting with the base year 1999-
2000. The Eleventh Finance Commission maintains that the State is expected 
to take effective steps for revenue augmentation and expenditure 
compression over the five year period so as to achieve gross fiscal deficit of 
the States on an aggregate to fall to 2.5% of GSDP; revenue deficit of all 
States, in aggregate, falling to zero; an d, interest payments as a percentage 
bf revenue receipts of the State sector, as a whole, to 18 to 20%. 
Madam, the Eleventh Finance Commission, in its supplementary 
Report said that the increase in wages and salaries should not exceed 5% or 
the increase in the consumer price index , whichever is higher; the increase in 
interest payment may be limited to 10% per  year. Again, it said that explicit
